overview: This file brings together reports and policy correspondence concerning the monitoring of Japanese merchant and naval shipping during 1940, especially tankers carrying Mexican crude oil from Tuxpan to Japan and the Navy Department’s effort to establish rapid worldwide reporting of Japanese vessel movements. Individual telegrams record the arrivals and departures of the Toei Maru, Sinkoku Maru, Nitiei Maru, and Omurosan Maru, while cross-reference sheets point to intelligence on other Japanese ships in Central and South American waters. The larger administrative sequence documents negotiations between the State and Navy Departments over reporting thresholds, cable costs, consular workloads, public-source collection, and the diplomatic danger of provoking Japanese suspicion. The bundle also contains later follow-up material from January and June 1941 and an anomalous or misfiled 1949 attaché-report page.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Collins on the Toei Maru’s departure from Tuxpan
subfiles.about: Reports the Toei Maru sailing from Tuxpan with crude oil for Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Collins reports that the Japanese tanker Toei Maru left Tuxpan on April 28 carrying 89,000 barrels of crude oil. Its declared route was to Yokohama through the Panama Canal, and the information was sent to the Navy and Coast Guard.

subfiles.title: Department note questioning confirmation of the original report
subfiles.to: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Notes that an apparent original report had not been confirmed.
subfiles.summary: This brief internal note states that the preceding item appears to be the original report and that nobody had confirmed it. It was routed to the Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs on June 17.

subfiles.title: Attaché’s report cover sheet on Japanese political forces
subfiles.about: A fragmentary attaché-report sheet identifies its subject as political forces in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The page is a heavily annotated attaché-report cover or fragment bearing serial number 104-59 and the subject “Japan Political Forces.” Its 1949 date and unrelated subject suggest that it may be an anomalous or misfiled page within the shipping file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to information on the fishing vessel Amano
subfiles.about: Points to a letter concerning the Japanese fishing vessel Amano in Costa Rican waters.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a letter filed under 818.00-W/115. That letter reportedly contains information about the activities of the Japanese fishing vessel Amano in Costa Rican waters.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornibrook’s despatch on the Norfolk Maru and Amano
subfiles.about: References a Costa Rican despatch about the Norfolk Maru and the Japanese-owned Amano.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to despatch 2469 concerning the Japanese merchant ship Norfolk Maru, seen alongside the Amano. It describes the Amano as Costa Rican-registered but Japanese-owned and almost wholly Japanese-crewed, and notes memoranda supplied by George Gordon and Vice Consul Ben Zweig.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Neal on the Sinkoku Maru’s arrival at Tuxpan
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival in ballast of the Japanese tanker Sinkoku Maru at Tuxpan.
subfiles.summary: Neal reports that the Sinkoku Maru arrived at Tuxpan on September 25 from Yokohama via Los Angeles and Cristóbal. The tanker was in ballast and expected to depart for Japanese ports through the Panama Canal; the message was transmitted to the Navy and Coast Guard.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Neal on the Sinkoku Maru’s departure
subfiles.about: Reports the Sinkoku Maru sailing from Tuxpan with crude oil for Tokuyama.
subfiles.summary: The Sinkoku Maru departed Tuxpan on September 26 for Tokuyama with 87,000 barrels of crude oil. The cargo was consigned for Taiheiyo Sekiyu K. Kaisha, and the report was forwarded to the Navy and Coast Guard.

subfiles.title: Liaison Office note on missing reports from Japanese ports
subfiles.about: Relays McCollum’s concern that no vessel-movement reports had arrived from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Commander McCollum told the Liaison Office that no reports on Japanese vessels from Japan had reached his attention. He argued that the system required departure reports from ports such as Yokohama and Kobe and asked Wilson to discuss the matter with him.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on cable costs and economical distribution of reporting instructions
subfiles.from: Division of Foreign Service Administration, M. P. Davis
subfiles.to: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office, Mr. Wilson
subfiles.about: Proposes cost and routing changes to the Navy’s worldwide ship-reporting request.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum warns that the requested cable traffic could be expensive and recommends charging the Navy under Foreign Service Regulations. It suggests routing reports from consular agents through supervising offices and dropping several direct recipients to reduce costs. It also warns that collection inside the Japanese Empire could require extra personnel and prove delicate in light of the Matsuo case.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note proposing a revised telegram to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Records preparation of a revised instruction to Tokyo after Ballantine’s conversation with McCollum.
subfiles.summary: Following the November 25 conversation between Commander McCollum and Joseph Ballantine, Far Eastern Affairs drafted a telegram to the Embassy at Tokyo. The draft was intended to satisfy the Navy’s needs without prejudicing the position of American consuls in Japan.

subfiles.title: Morris note on dispatching and redrafting vessel-reporting telegrams
subfiles.to: Miss Moore, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Authorizes the Tokyo telegram while requiring the other proposed telegrams to be redrafted.
subfiles.summary: Morris states that Wilson approved sending the telegram to Tokyo. The other telegrams were removed for redrafting in accordance with the recommendations of Foreign Service Administration, after which the file was to return to the Liaison Office.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of the Ballantine–McCollum conversation
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records McCollum’s narrowed explanation of the Navy’s requirements for reports on Japanese shipping.
subfiles.summary: McCollum explained that the Navy tracked about 160 Japanese merchant vessels over 4,000 tons, but wanted reports on only roughly 50 or 60 engaged in relevant overseas services. He proposed routine telegraphic reporting when consuls issued bills of health, supplemented by publicly available departure information. He dropped the request for most naval-vessel reporting and argued that consuls could cover Kobe and other ports more effectively than the small Naval Attaché staff; Ballantine agreed to refer the modified proposal to his superiors.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs objections to the proposed Tokyo instruction
subfiles.about: Argues that the original instruction to consuls in Japan would be diplomatically risky and should not be sent.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs warns that singling out Japanese vessels and including naval ships would arouse Japanese suspicion and could impair the usefulness of American consuls. It recommends limiting attention to merchant vessels in trans-Pacific and Philippine trade and suggests that the Naval Attaché use shipping-association schedules and published press notices. The memorandum concludes that collection through the attaché would be no harder and substantially less likely to create diplomatic trouble.

subfiles.title: Note on missing consular representation at Mombasa and Borneo
subfiles.about: Explains why Mombasa and Borneo could not be included in a draft reporting telegram.
subfiles.summary: The note records that the Department lacked consular representation at Mombasa, Kenya Colony, and in Borneo. Those locations therefore could not be included among the posts receiving the Navy-requested reporting instructions.

subfiles.title: Circular telegram establishing reports on Japanese vessel movements
subfiles.to: American Consul at Batavia and listed consular offices
subfiles.about: Directs consular posts to cable publicly available movement data on large Japanese commercial vessels and Japanese naval vessels.
subfiles.summary: The circular orders reporting when bills of health were issued to Japanese commercial vessels of 4,000 gross tons or more and to Japanese naval vessels, including arrival and departure dates, last ports, and destinations. It also requests published departure information for comparable ships bound outside the United States and charges the expense to the Navy. The continuation distributes the order to posts across Australia, New Zealand, the Caribbean, South Africa, India, Ceylon, the Bahamas, and Singapore, with instructions for subordinate consulates or agents.

subfiles.title: Telegram instructing the American Consul at Belize
subfiles.about: Directs Belize to cable movement information on large Japanese merchant ships and naval vessels.
subfiles.summary: This separately worded instruction requests arrival, departure, ship-name, destination, and last-port information when bills of health are issued to qualifying Japanese vessels. It also calls for reports based on press or other public information and directs that the Navy pay the cable costs.

subfiles.title: Telegram suspending ship-movement reports from Cape Town
subfiles.about: Suspends the earlier consular ship-reporting instructions because the Naval Attaché was reporting directly.
subfiles.summary: The Department tells Cape Town to suspend the ship-movement instructions issued in December 1940 and January 1941. A Naval Attaché was by then furnishing the information directly to the Navy Department by cipher.

subfiles.title: Letter informing Frank Knox that reporting instructions had been issued
subfiles.to: Frank Knox, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Confirms that Foreign Service officers had been instructed to report Japanese vessel movements by cable.
subfiles.summary: The letter answers Admiral Stark’s October 28 request for faster intelligence on Japanese shipping. It informs Secretary Knox that the appropriate officers had received telegraphic instructions and that their reports would be forwarded promptly to the Navy Department.

subfiles.title: Liaison Office routing sheet
subfiles.about: A largely blank routing page bearing reference numbers.
subfiles.summary: The page contains the Liaison Office heading and a short sequence of routing or reference numbers, with most entries struck through. It provides no substantive discussion but appears to have accompanied the surrounding correspondence.

subfiles.title: Admiral Stark’s request for worldwide cable reports on Japanese shipping
subfiles.about: Requests systematic radio or cable reports on major Japanese commercial and naval vessels from designated regions worldwide.
subfiles.summary: Stark explains that changes in Japanese merchant-marine operations might provide advance warning of political developments affecting United States–Japanese relations. Because wartime disruptions had made mailed reports and published schedules inadequate, he requests rapid reports of vessel names, arrivals, departures, previous ports, and destinations. The proposed network covers the Americas, West Indies, Netherlands East Indies, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, India, Ceylon, southern and eastern Africa, and the Japanese Empire.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to the Sakura Maru’s meeting with the Belgoland
subfiles.about: References a report that the Sakura Maru met the German steamship Belgoland outside territorial waters.
subfiles.summary: Captain Boy reportedly stated that the Japanese steamer Sakura Maru met the German steamship Belgoland outside territorial waters on October 26. The Sakura Maru arrived at Barranquilla on October 29 and cleared for New York that same day.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Collins on the Nitiei Maru’s departure
subfiles.about: Reports the Nitiei Maru leaving Tuxpan with crude oil for Tokuyama.
subfiles.summary: Collins reports that the Japanese tanker Nitiei Maru cleared Tuxpan on November 18 carrying 87,000 barrels of crude oil for Tokuyama. Its clearance did not state whether it would travel through the Panama Canal, and the report was repeated to the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Simplex-printer transmission instruction for the Navy Department
subfiles.about: Instructs staff to transmit an associated message to the Navy Department by Simplex printer.
subfiles.summary: This administrative slip directs transmission of the accompanying ship report to the Navy Department by Simplex printer. It also requests that the sending time be endorsed on the copy before its return to the Liaison Office.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of the Nitiei Maru telegram
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report of the Nitiei Maru’s departure from Tuxpan.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the November 19 telegram reporting that the Nitiei Maru left Tuxpan with 87,000 barrels of crude oil for Tokuyama. It again notes that the clearance did not specify use of the Panama Canal and that the Embassy had been informed.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Collins on the Omurosan Maru’s departure
subfiles.about: Reports the Omurosan Maru sailing from Tuxpan with crude oil for Tokuyama.
subfiles.summary: Collins reports that the Omurosan Maru left Tuxpan on November 27 carrying 73,000 barrels of crude oil for Tokuyama. The ship’s clearance did not show whether it would use the Panama Canal, and the report was sent to the Navy and Coast Guard.

subfiles.title: Confidential telegram directing reports from consuls in Japan
subfiles.about: Asks the Embassy to instruct consuls in Japan to report departures of large Japanese merchant and public vessels.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks the Embassy, unless it perceives objections, to have consuls report the names and destinations of Japanese merchant and public vessels of 4,000 gross tons or more when issuing bills of health. Consuls were also to report publicly available information on overseas departures, with the Navy charged for cable expenses.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to copper shipments aboard Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: References information on copper shipments to Japan aboard three Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to despatch 108 concerning copper shipments to Japan. It specifically names the Wales Maru of Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, the Rakuyo Maru of Nippon Yusen Kaisha, and the Noto Maru.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to K.K.K. Line calls at Puntarenas
subfiles.about: References information on regular calls by Japanese K.K.K. Line ships at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch states that K.K.K. Line merchant ships regularly called at Puntarenas to load and unload freight and passengers. It adds that probably no more than one Japanese-flag vessel was present in port at any one time.

subfiles.title: Liaison Office note clarifying the Navy’s need for actual departure reports
subfiles.from: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office, B. A. B.
subfiles.about: Records McCollum’s clarification that the Navy wanted actual departures, not vessel schedules.
subfiles.summary: After telephoning Commander McCollum, the author reports that the Navy did not want shipping schedules telegraphed but did want information on actual Japanese vessel departures. McCollum also said that existing State Department teletyping procedures could continue, with the Navy arranging internal delivery to the Office of Naval Intelligence.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how routine consular paperwork—bills of health, clearances, press notices, and port observations—was being converted into a worldwide naval-intelligence system before Pearl Harbor. Its juxtaposition of precise tanker movements and cargo quantities with internal arguments over cost, staffing, and Japanese suspicion reveals both the strategic value and diplomatic hazards of maritime surveillance. The proposed 4,000-ton threshold, named reporting regions, and discussion of approximately 50–60 relevant overseas vessels provide unusually concrete evidence of the Navy’s collection priorities. The later suspension message, cross-references to encounters and commodity shipments, and anomalous 1949 page also illuminate how the decimal-file system accumulated follow-ups, duplicates, routing material, and occasional filing irregularities.
